# Kururin Squash!

**Kururin Squash!** (Japanese: くるりんスカッシュ!, Hepburn: *Kururin Sukasshu!*) is an action-puzzle video game developed by Eighting and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It was released exclusively in Japan on October 14, 2004 . It is the third and final installment in the *Kururin* series, following *Kuru Kuru Kururin* (2001) and *Kururin Paradise* (2002) for the Game Boy Advance .

The game retains the core gameplay of its predecessors, where the player pilots a slowly rotating stick called the Helirin through narrow, maze-like courses without touching the walls. *Kururin Squash!* is the first and only title in the series to feature 3D computer graphics, although the gameplay remains on a two-dimensional plane . The game introduces new mechanics such as boss battles, underwater segments, and specialized vehicles that possess unique abilities like punching or shooting projectiles .

Upon release, *Kururin Squash!* received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its visual style, music, and gameplay mechanics. However, it faced criticism regarding its difficulty level relative to previous entries and its short length . Commercially, the game performed poorly, selling fewer than 20,000 copies in Japan by the end of 2004, making it the lowest-selling entry in the franchise . Despite never being officially localized for international markets, it has been cited as a cult classic and an import-friendly title due to its low language barrier .

## Gameplay

*Kururin Squash!* is a puzzle game requiring precise timing and navigation. The player controls the Helirin, a vehicle resembling a long, rotating stick. The primary objective is to guide the Helirin from the start of a maze to the goal without colliding with walls or obstacles .

### Core Mechanics
The Helirin rotates automatically at a constant speed. The player uses the GameCube controller's analog stick to move the vehicle through the stage. The "A" button is typically used to activate special vehicle abilities, while other buttons can increase the movement speed or the rotation speed of the Helirin to navigate tight corners .

The game utilizes a health system represented by hearts. By default, the Helirin has three hearts. Colliding with a wall or an enemy results in the loss of one heart and a time penalty. If all hearts are lost, the Helirin shatters, and the player must restart the stage or resume from the last checkpoint . Blue springs scattered throughout levels reverse the direction of the Helirin's rotation when touched .

Unlike the 2D sprite-based graphics of the Game Boy Advance titles, *Kururin Squash!* uses 3D polygonal graphics. This allows for visual depth, such as transparency effects where players can see background elements beneath the maze .

### New Features and Vehicles
*Kururin Squash!* introduces several new gameplay elements to the series. Coins are scattered throughout each stage; collecting all coins in a level contributes to a "perfect" rating and adds to a total count used to purchase items in the in-game shop . Shop items include new Helirin skins, interface designs, and "super play" demonstration videos .

The game features "Action Helirins," which are specialized vehicles used in specific stages to overcome unique environmental hazards. These include:
* **Helibokaan:** Equipped with boxing gloves that extend when the player presses a button, allowing the vehicle to break obstacles and punch enemies .
* **Helibashan:** A submarine-like vehicle used in water levels. It can dive underwater to avoid surface obstacles or navigate submerged tunnels .
* **Heliburuun:** Capable of generating tornadoes. These tornadoes can defeat enemies, clear smoke, or block fire hazards .
* **Helibibyuun:** Features lasers that shoot from the ends of the stick to destroy enemies or trigger switches .
* **Heliboboh:** A vehicle that emits flamethrowers to defeat enemies .

Boss battles are included at the end of each world. These encounters require the player to utilize the specific Action Helirin introduced in that world to deplete the boss's health meter .

### Modes
The game features several modes:
* **Adventure Mode:** The main story campaign where players progress through different worlds, unlocking new stages and vehicles .
* **Challenge Mode:** A mode focused on completing stages as quickly as possible .
* **Multiplayer:** The game supports up to four players in split-screen. "Race Mode" involves players competing to finish a course first, while "Battle Mode" requires players to collect coins and use weapons to attack opponents in an arena setting .

## Plot

The story is set in the fictional Rin Village. The protagonist, Kururin, wins a grand prize in a local lottery: a "4 Nights and 5 Days Family Tour of 4 Countries." Kururin and his extensive family—including his parents, Totorin and Kakarin, and his many siblings—depart for the vacation .

The family visits four distinct locations: Sweet Island (a land of sweets), Natural World (forests and seas), Snowscape (a snowy region), and Future Vision (a futuristic city). However, upon returning home, Kururin discovers that only he, his father Totorin, and his mother Kakarin have returned. His siblings are missing. It is revealed that the antagonist, Professor Isogashima, has kidnapped the siblings and created robots to prevent Kururin from interfering with his research .

Kururin sets out in the Helirin to rescue his siblings across the four worlds. After saving them, he returns home to find that his father, Totorin, has also been kidnapped by Isogashima and taken to the Wonderverse, the final world. Kururin travels to the Wonderverse, defeats the Professor, and rescues his father, reuniting the family .

## Development

*Kururin Squash!* was developed by Eighting, a Japanese studio primarily known for fighting games such as *Bloody Roar* and *Battle Stadium D.O.N* . It was published by Nintendo. The game was produced by Hiroshi Sato and Masato Toyoshima, with direction by Shinji Hatano and Tomonori Fujisawa .

The game marks the series' transition from handheld consoles to a home console, utilizing the GameCube's hardware to render 3D graphics while maintaining the 2D gameplay plane. The visual style incorporates a "puppet theater" aesthetic for cutscenes, where characters appear as 2D cardboard cutouts on sticks .

Yōichi Kotabe returned as the character designer for the game. This was the final title Kotabe worked on in this capacity at Nintendo before leaving the company in 2007 . The soundtrack was composed by Atsuhiro Motoyama, who had previously worked on the *Umihara Kawase* series .

*Kururin Squash!* was officially revealed in *Famitsu* magazine in August 2004 and was released in Japan on October 14, 2004 . Unlike the first game in the series, *Kuru Kuru Kururin*, which saw a release in Europe and Australia, *Kururin Squash!* was never released outside of Japan .

## Reception

### Critical Response
*Kururin Squash!* received generally positive reviews from import-focused media outlets. Critics praised the game's presentation, particularly the transition to 3D. *Nintendo World Report* highlighted the "fantastic graphics," noting the particle and lighting effects, as well as the unique "puppet on a stick" art style used in cutscenes . The music by Atsuhiro Motoyama was described as "marvelously constructed and quite soothing" .

The gameplay was commended for its responsiveness, with the GameCube's analog stick providing "pinpoint accuracy" compared to the D-pad controls of the Game Boy Advance titles . The introduction of new vehicles and boss battles was seen as a welcome expansion of the formula. *Eurogamer* noted that while the basic puzzle levels were the most satisfying, the variations provided by the new vehicles had their moments .

However, the game faced criticism regarding its difficulty and content volume. *Eurogamer* stated that the game "doesn't push you hard enough or for long enough," suggesting that the new levels were not as "pure and addictive" as the straightforward puzzles of the predecessors . *Hardcore Gaming 101* noted that while the game is fun, the Adventure mode is relatively short, and the multiplayer battle mode was preferred over the race mode .

### Sales
Commercially, *Kururin Squash!* was not successful. In its debut week in Japan, it reached number 18 on the sales charts, selling approximately 5,745 copies . It dropped off the charts quickly, selling a total of 18,562 copies by the end of 2004 . It was the lowest-selling entry in the *Kururin* series and one of Nintendo's lowest-selling first-party titles on the GameCube in Japan .

### Legacy
Despite its low sales and lack of international release, *Kururin Squash!* is considered a "cult classic" among GameCube enthusiasts . It is frequently recommended as an import title for Western collectors because the game features very little Japanese text that is essential for gameplay, making it accessible to non-Japanese speakers .

5.content:
Kuru Kuru Kururin debuted for both the Japanese and European Game Boy Advance launches. The idea was deceptively simple -- all you have to do was guide a constantly rotating stick through a maze and reach the goal without hitting any obstacles. Doing so makes you lose time and health. Three hits and you have to start again. Kururin Squash is the third game in the series, and as such, it expands on this basic idea of navigating your way through a maze. In addition to the standard helicopter, you're now able to guide specially designed helicopters that allow you to punch, dive, shoot flames and throw tornados.

As mentioned in my [impressions](http://www.planetgamecube.com/impressions.cfm?action=profile&id=716), the first thing that will strike you about the game is the incredible graphic style. (Take a look at the intro, which is available for [download](http://www.planetgamecube.com/news.cfm?action=item&id=5745) to see for yourself.) The graphics are crisp and bright, and all the characters in cutscenes are moved around as though they were puppets on sticks, with additional sticks used for controlling their arms. If they want to change expressions, the character will flip around and a completely different version of the same character will be on the other side. It's a really refreshing look, and I've never seen anything like it before.

The levels themselves are fully polygonal, which is a massive leap from the 2D (but still excellent) sprite graphics of the previous games. The mazes have some great transparency effects that allow you to see, for example, forests with butterflies underneath you. Other high points for the GameCube version are the lighting and particle effects. It's quite strange to see such great effects in a puzzle game, but there they are. Dust will kick up when you punch walls, lasers will leave light halos, and there are surprisingly massive explosions for destroying enemies. Enemies caught in tornados will be spun high in the air and fly right towards the camera. The effects are subtle, but very pretty.

The game's soundtrack is quite decent. Although the music tracks clock in at around a minute before they begin to loop, they're pleasant enough for you not to notice. There're a large variety of instruments used, including a very Seventies-like "wikky-wa" guitar melody when you successfully complete a level. Each level's music suits its area - the sky levels have airy, futuristic music, the ocean level music is wonderfully mellow, and the boss theme is suitably frantic. Most of the sound effects are strikingly similar to the Game Boy Advance games, which is not a problem, as it keeps a sense of familiarity. Most other sounds are similar to typical video-game sounds, but it's wonderfully satisfying to hear the "whoosh" of the flamethrower Heririn (or helicopter). The only problem that I have with the game's sound are the noises used for the character speech. It's a kind of high-pitched tweeting, and because I use headphones a lot, it rattles right through my brain.

Kururin Squash mixes elements from the previous games -- that is, the guiding of a constantly rotating stick through a maze without hitting anything -- and adds new helicopters that cause the player to think a bit more carefully when guiding them. The Punch Heririn can be used to destroy obstacles and enemies, but you get a bit of recoil from it, so you need to allow a little leeway when you use it. The Dive Heririn will cause you to think on two different levels, as you'll have to play through sections of levels which need to be quickly navigated by rising and submerging again, in some cases fighting strong currents and whirlpools. The Flame Heririn makes things incredibly tough, as the levels take place entirely on-rails. Using the Control Stick will freely rotate the Heririn, and you'll occasionally need to dodge precariously placed crystals and massive enemies that chase you throughout the level. The Tornado Heririn also allows for some clever puzzles. Some will see you temporarily blocking an enemy dispenser; others will have you safely riding in a tornado as you launch it down a corridor full of flamethrowers. You'll also need to learn to use those special Heririns for clever boss battles. Eighting have gone all-out in using the GameCube to create an expanded Kururin experience.

Kururin Squash is also the first game in the series to introduce currency. Strewn throughout the stages are gold coins -- collect all of them in a stage in addition to not getting hurt at all and you'll earn yourself a perfect clear. Coins can also be earned by defeating enemies. You won't need to collect those, as they'll be collected automatically. Coins can be used in the various shops on the map screen (the Carnies from Kururin Paradise make cameo appearances in running the shops), where you'll be able to purchase various items. They include world maps, a GBA to GC Link Up Mini-Game, additional Heririns, Customizable HUDs, and Teacher Hare Movies that show you how to beat the stages safely. Some of the Heririns include a Chocolate Bar, a Tank, and a Heririn with Nintendo logo blades that plays the Super Mario Bros. coin sound when you press the horn. Collecting all of the shop items is purely optional, but it makes for a good reason to return to the game.

The Battle Multiplayer in Squash definitely seems to be more fun than the Race Mode. In Race, avid Kururin players have a distinct advantage over novices, whereas with Battle it's all about beating each other up, powering up, and collecting the most coins. The tables can quickly turn if you have the right power up. In Race, although the leader gets a handicap of becoming larger, they can easily overcome this if they're a skilled player. The GBA to GC link-up game is basically just a memory match game, which is a bit of a shame.

The biggest injustice is that this will be the third Kururin game to not see the light of day outside of Japan. It's totally bizarre as to why, as the game represents everything that Nintendo could possibly want -- a simple, yet fun concept, a new franchise, and a game that can be played without having to worry about the language barrier. If you like your puzzle games and have not heard of the Kururin series before, I'd **highly** recommend getting this game. Actually, I'd recommend all three, as they're all stellar games. Kururin Squash continues the series' legacy of great fun, lastability, and typical Japanese wackiness. As an import game, the language barrier is zilch. Pick it up from our partners at [Lik-Sang](http://www.lik-sang.com/info.php?category=79&products_id=5407&) now!

_**Kururin Squash!**_[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-2) is a 2004 [puzzle video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puzzle_video_game "Puzzle video game") developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting") and published by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"). It was released exclusively in Japan on October 14, 2004. _Kururin Squash!_ is the third and final game in the _Kururin_ series as well as the first entry on a home console, following the release of _[Kuru Kuru Kururin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuru_Kuru_Kururin "Kuru Kuru Kururin")_ (2001) and _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ (2002) on the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). The game uses [3D graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"), with 2D artwork of its characters being used on cardboard cutouts outside of gameplay.

_Kururin Squash!_ is a maze navigation game where the player attempts to reach the goal at the end for a high score. It introduces coins, enemies, and bosses in its levels, with multiple new vehicles being used to overcome specific obstacles. _Kururin Squash!_ received generally positive reviews from critics for its gameplay, visuals, and style, with mixed opinions on its difficulty. It is considered to be one of the best Japanese-exclusive GameCube games. Selling less than 20,000 copies, it is the lowest-selling _Kururin_ game, and it is Nintendo's second worst-performing GameCube game in Japan.

[![Image 3: This screenshot shows the Helibokaan flying in a circular arena, attacking the barrier protecting Professor Isogashima. The game's interface displays the time, coin counter score, and Kururin with all three of his hearts remaining.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/17/Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg/250px-Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash_Boss_Fight_Screenshot.jpg)

Kururin piloting the Helibokaan during the [boss fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_/(video_games/) "Boss (video games)") against Professor Isogashima in the first world.

The player controls Kururin, a bird who pilots the Helirin, a constantly spinning helicopter, by navigating [mazes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze "Maze") while avoiding walls and other obstacles. The player can hold down buttons on the [GameCube controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_controller "GameCube controller") to adjust the speed at which the Helirin spins and the speed of the Helirin itself.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3) Kururin has three hearts by default, and each stage contains checkpoints where their hearts can be refilled.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) If the player hits any obstacles, they lose a heart, and three seconds are added to the in-game timer, with the goal being to complete each stage in the least amount of time for a high score.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5) In the single-player mode, the player can select whether to control a larger or more compact Helirin, a method of adjusting difficulty.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) Two modes are available from the start, the Adventure mode with the stages and story, as well as a Challenge mode where the player attempts to complete the stages as fast as possible.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) After completing the Adventure mode, a third mode is unlocked where the player controls the center sphere of the Helirin, which does not feature the rotating helicopter blades, but can't stop moving.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-8) After completing this mode, the Extra mode is unlocked, featuring rotated versions of the stages.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-9)

_Kururin Squash!_ introduces new vehicles, enemies in stages, and [boss fights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_/(video_games/) "Boss (video games)") at the end of each world. The "Action Helirins" are helicopters that provide various advantages the standard Helirin does not. One of these vehicles is the Helibokaan,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-10) which is a helicopter that can break obstacles and punch enemies. The Helibashan can dive underwater to avoid obstacles on the surface, the Heliboboh can shoot fire when attached to rails, the Heliburuun can create whirlwinds, and the Helibibyuun can shoot objects using rapid fire.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-11)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 12–13  The single-player modes feature several unique worlds, with every few stages taking place in a new environment.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 28–29  Coins are present in every stage, and collecting all the coins will net the player a perfect bonus, increasing their total coin counter.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Euro-13) Coins can be used in shops, which contain many useful items and accessories. These items can increase the player's hearts, respawn them at the beginning after they lose their hearts, or provide a minimap for stages. The shop also contains movies that can guide the player on how to complete individual levels,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3) with shops being run by members of the Magic Group, the false antagonists from _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 21

The multiplayer in _Kururin Squash!_ has two modes that support up to four players. The Race Mode has over forty obstacle courses where players attempt to reach the end while hitting opponents into walls or blocking their opponents' vehicles, taking place on stages from the Challenge mode.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) In the Battle Mode, players can fight on ten unique stages by using power-ups and weapons that is similar to [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame") from [_Super Monkey Ball_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Monkey_Ball_/(video_game/) "Super Monkey Ball (video game)").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15) The objective for this mode is to collect the most coins while attacking other players.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) By connecting a [GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_%E2%80%93_Game_Boy_Advance_link_cable "GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable"), up to four [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") systems can play a [spot the difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spot_the_difference "Spot the difference")\-type quiz game, which can be purchased from the shop.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)

The story is told through a [paper puppet theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy_theater "Toy theater") style, which received praise from critics.

After Kururin wins the lottery for his family, they travel across the four continents of the world. However, upon arriving back to their home in Kururin Village, only the parents of the family return. After losing track of his family members, Kururin goes on an adventure to find them across the four continents.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 6–7  Throughout the journey, Kururin's guide, Teacher Hare, provides him with new Action Helirins that help him progress through the different worlds.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Manual-5): 12–13  Kururin travels to face Professor Isogashima, a mad inventor bird who has captured all the members of his family since they interfered with his research, and he releases them after being defeated in boss battles.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-16) Professor Isogashima and his Isogashimachines serve as the main antagonists with the goal of making everyone else busy.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-17) Once Kururin returns home after rescuing his siblings, he discovers that his parents were also kidnapped by Professor Isogashima, so he travels to the fifth and final world in space to rescue them.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-18) When defeated, Professor Isogashima crash lands on their home planet, makes himself busy by fixing the problems caused by his Isogashimachines, and the Kururin family returns home.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-19)

_Kururin Squash!_ was developed by [Eighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighting "Eighting"), and was the first game in the _Kururin_ series to transition from 2D to [3D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"). The directors and producers from _[Kururin Paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Paradise "Kururin Paradise")_ returned to work on _Kururin Squash!_ as the final entry in the series. [Yōichi Kotabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y%C5%8Dichi_Kotabe "Yōichi Kotabe") returns as the series' character designer, with it being the final game he serves that role at Nintendo prior to his departure from the company in 2007.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Credits-20) It was officially revealed in an issue of _[Famitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famitsu "Famitsu")_ magazine on August 5, 2004,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-21) and later released on October 14, 2004. It had a small advertising campaign, with a publication in a column of _[Nintendo Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Dream "Nintendo Dream")_ and commercials that used the Helirin as a prop.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-23) In a developer interview with [Yuichi Toyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuichi_Toyama "Yuichi Toyama") and Kenichi Yokoo for _[Sōkyūgurentai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Diver "Terra Diver")_ and _[Mahou Daisakusen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorcer_Striker "Sorcer Striker")_, Yokoo cited _Kururin Squash!_ as his favorite non-arcade game he worked on.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-24) Eighting would later collaborate with Nintendo on the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") game _[Master of Illusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Illusion_/(video_game/) "Master of Illusion (video game)")_ in 2006.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-25)

_Kururin Squash!_ received generally positive reviews,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GameStats-31) with praise for the 3D visuals,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) music,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) as well as improved gameplay and controls from its predecessors.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) The art style received praise, with colorful 3D environments and stylized cutscenes represented by cardboard puppets on sticks, creating a unique and refreshing style.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWRPrev-32)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) The multiplayer modes were also complimented for their quality. Caleb Gossler of _Nintendojo_ claimed _Kururin Squash!_ to have "some of the best four-player party games on the GameCube".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Nintendojo-12) Chandra Nair of _[GamesTM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesTM "GamesTM")_ described the levels as "cunningly designed", complimenting them for taking advantage of the different abilities of the Action Helirins.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GTM-27) Ben Kosmina of _Nintendo World Report_ described the overall experience as stellar, complimenting the title for having a low language barrier to enjoy the gameplay, despite its exclusivity to Japan.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWR-4) Similarly, Nadia Grace Mullings of _Game Rant_ claimed it to be "worthy of being one of the best GameCube titles, despite it having never been released in America".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:1-33) Anoop Gantayat of _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ expressed interest in _Kururin Squash!_ releasing overseas due to the addictive gameplay, even if there were no plans to do so by [Nintendo of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_of_America "Nintendo of America").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:0-6) The low price was also praised, with _[Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_/(magazine/) "Edge (magazine)")_ magazine describing the price point as enticing.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-34)

The main criticism of _Kururin Squash!_ was its difficulty and short length. In comparison to the Game Boy Advance titles which featured more challenging stages, _Kururin Squash!_ contains generally easier levels that could be completed faster due to the improvement in movement accuracy, as a result of switching from a [d-pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad "D-pad") to the GameCube control stick.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-HardcoreGaming101-3)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-GTM-Mag-26)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Euro-13)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) Despite this critique, others have claimed the difficulty level is still present. Jonti Davies of _Kikizo_ described the gameplay as "straightforward in principle, but, in later stages especially, often devilishly difficult in practice".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Kikizo-15) Ollie Reynolds of _Nintendo Life_ shared this sentiment, noting how navigating the mazes can become "incredibly tense" as the player progresses.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:2-35) _[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ later retracted this criticism, with Keza MacDonald stating that it hardly affects the overall experience, considering _Kururin Squash!_ a [cult classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_video_game "Cult video game") on the GameCube.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) Additionally, critics were disappointed by the lack of multiplayer modes, in comparison to the multiple [minigames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame") introduced in _Kururin Paradise_. Ben Kosmina of _Nintendo World Report_ considered the fewer number of multiplayer offerings disappointing.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-NWRPrev-32) Writers for _Edge_ magazine claimed the sixteen minigames from _Kururin Paradise_ were better than having only two in _Kururin Squash!_, with the Game Boy Advance link cable minigame being referred to as "no more than a novelty".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Edge-7) In retrospective reviews, _Kururin Squash!_ has been cited as one of the best Japanese-exclusive GameCube games,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:1-33)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-37)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-Cult_Classics-14) with many desiring an English localization.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-38)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-:2-35)

In Japan, _Kururin Squash!_ reached the eighteenth position on sales charts during its initial launch week, selling 5,745 copies.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-39) It only placed among the top thirty weekly video game sales one additional time the following week.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-40) _Kururin Squash!_ sold a total of 18,562 copies in Japan from release to December 20, 2004.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-41) It was the third lowest-selling GameCube game in 2004 and the second lowest-selling first-party game behind [_Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternal_Darkness "Eternal Darkness"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-42) subsequently making it the lowest-selling entry in the _Kururin_ series, despite being sold at a budget price comparative to other GameCube titles.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-release-1)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-43)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!#cite_note-44)

The player controls a slowly spinning stick called the Helirin, and must maneuver it through a series of mazes without touching the walls. If the stick hits any wall or dangerous object three times it will shatter, forcing the player to start over again. The player controls the stick's direction and 3 levels of speed, but the continual rotation of the stick makes the task difficult. Bonus points are awarded once the player has successfully completed a level, and a gold star for completing the level without any crashes. The game also records shortest times taken to beat each level.

The game starts off with simple training levels, where instructions are given on how to play and get around the first corners. After this tutorial there are eight [stages](https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Kururin_Squash!/Stages "Kururin Squash!/Stages") in each stage which progressively increase in difficulty and length.

Stage objectives

*   **Puzzle mode:** The main objective is to collect coins.
*   **Race mode:** To finish each maze within a target time frame.
*   **Multiplayer:** Up to 4 players compete in a split-screen frenzy.
*   **Battle mode:** Up to 4 players must collect coins while holding off their opponents with various weapons.

New features\[[edit](https://strategywiki.org/w/index.php?title=Kururin_Squash!/Gameplay&veaction=edit&section=1 "Edit section: New features") | [edit source](https://strategywiki.org/w/index.php?title=Kururin_Squash!/Gameplay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: New features")\]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unlike the previous titles of the series, **Kururin Squash!** introduces water levels with [power-ups](https://strategywiki.org/w/index.php?title=Kururin_Squash!/Power-ups&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kururin Squash!/Power-ups (page does not exist)") that make the Helirin work like a submarine, use guns, punch with boxing gloves, create tornadoes, or use flame-throwers. Bosses are also present at the end of each stage.

Ah, this takes us back. School fetes, manoeuvring rings around twisty wire mazes without sounding a buzzer, perspiration accumulating in the furrows of our infant brow as we overcome the trickiest sections, and the eventual consolation of an "Aw, so close!" when our trademark steadiness eventually fails us and the buzzer cruelly sounds. We'd swear blind they magnetised bits of the wire to save on the lollypop prize budget. But we still wanted another go.

Kururin, in its various forms, is not much more than an update of that buzz bar idea. The goal is to direct a perpetually spinning stick around mazes using the analogue control without touching the sides or any of the course obstacles more than twice. With only a few health-replenishing spinny flower icons dotted throughout each level, and only the option to vary the speed of the stick-spin using the right shoulder button, any gamer can easily imagine how it challenges and how it locks you in with its charming simplicity.

Sticky situations
-----------------

![Image 1](https://www.eurogamer.net/1_p6HTjI1.jpg)

As it's grown from this simple template across three instalments (the first of which, Kuru Kuru Kururin, was among the first wave of Western GBA titles), Kururin has introduced other goals and quirks to the reaction-driven template. You also have to think about collecting 100 per cent of any given level's coins, spread around the play area and sometimes off the beaten track in side areas that involve risk as well as reward, and as we arrive at this Cube instalment, we discover that Nintendo's chosen developer Eighting has managed to expand the idea without separating it entirely from its charm, introducing variations like submersible craft, guns, boxing gloves, on-rails flamethrowing and even whirlwind-chucking and boss battles.

Playing it on anything larger than a 14" television is glorious overkill. The inescapable truth is that it would work just as well played on a Casio watch screen as long as the stick and the walls were distinct; the 3D backgrounds and bizarre, typically Japanese story sequences featuring our ducky hero and his hazard-prone adversaries are charming but totally unnecessary. And that's just as well, because sadly these new levels aren't as pure and addictive as straightforward Kururin puzzling, and as a result we'd recommend the series' previous offerings over this one, even if it were not because of Eighting's attempts to grow the formula.

But that's not to say that Kururin Squash is a bad example of a Kururin game by any stretch. The main puzzle mode, which features some 40 or so levels, never asks you to do more than get to the end without hitting the sides too much, even if it varies the manner in which you achieve this and likes to tease you with tricky-to-obtain loot whose precarious positioning threatens to undo the last few minutes worth of effort, and overall we had no qualms about sitting in front of this for several hours non-stop, just as we did with previous Kururin.

Duck and cover
--------------

![Image 2](https://www.eurogamer.net/2_wEo2Kx1.jpg)

Another option is a sort of 'race' mode where the challenge is not to collect loot and hitting the barriers is not such a worry, but instead the goal is to navigate similar but distinctly simpler Kururin mazes and hit the goal within the target time. To make things a bit less frustrating, these levels are also split up by regular checkpoints, to which you'll return if you take just two hits in any given section.

There's also a multiplayer mode that supports this manner of racing for up to four players in split-screen, which can be manic when your sticks are clanging together, and finally there's a deathmatch-ish mode, which treats the game's new abilities like the flamethrower and boxing gloves as short-burst power-ups in a competitive mode reminiscent of [Super Monkey Ball](https://www.eurogamer.net/games/super-monkey-ball)'s Monkey Target, where the goal is to finish up with the most coins by grabbing any that are strewn about and mashing your friends to mug them of their accumulated wealth.

Returning though to the leading light of the piece, the puzzle mode, it's pleasing to note that the level design can be as inventive as ever. Basic puzzle levels, featuring nothing more than a rotating stick, are definitely the most satisfying, as you strain to manoeuvre the spinning stick around tightly constructed mazes without incurring damage, using bounce pads to change the spin direction and avoid touching the sides, and dodging block-crushers and other moving obstacles at the same time. At its absolute best you'll be changing spin direction fluidly as you navigate tight, impossibly twisty pathways, and you'll emerge with a huge grin on your face. But, to be fair, the variations have their moments too. The submarine in particular, which brings with it the ability to dive underwater for a spell (the "water meter" in this case being the sight of the little ducky's icon in the bottom left gradually filling up with water as he pants and cries out) adds obvious depth, exploited by Eighting with mines and coins on the surface as well as underwater, various other surface obstacles like logs and a mixture of rapids and whirlpools to propel them - and you - around in a manner that demands more of your eager thumbs than regular levels.

Billed prominently
------------------

![Image 3](https://www.eurogamer.net/3_S9c35Rd.jpg)

Boxing gloves, meanwhile, allow you to smash up enemies (the more challenging of which herald some coinage and do not respawn), while the projectile-firing effort has you doing similar but with steadier streams of enemies to dodge (including ChuChu Rocket-style trains of what we think are mice, and, at its best, huge caterpillars barrelling after you like that rock in Raiders of the [Lost Ark](https://www.eurogamer.net/games/lost-ark)), and introduces mazes of green red blocks that bar the way and have to be excised by hunting down the destructible green blob which then blows the rest up along with any circling enemies in a flashy chain reaction. Hitting things with your projectiles is all the more difficult when you can't stop spinning, of course.

Then there are the whirlwind levels, which are some of the most traditionally puzzle-like, allowing you to charge up twisters by holding A and then unleash them in a chosen direction to strike at enemies, block off streams of fire, blow cloud cover out of the way, and spin large propellers that bar your progress; doing so also involves judging whether or not the movement of the blades will uncork flamethrowers that you can't dodge, and planning against such an eventuality.

Apart from one final spinny alternative, flamethrowing's the only other thing - and interestingly it's on rails, the idea being to spit flame (a beautiful effect, incidentally) by holding A and using the analogue stick to twist your chopper blade as you see fit to dodge track-side obstacles and enemies. You can speed up movement by holding B, which also extends reach of the fire, and Eighting often keeps you moving faster than you can really cope or pursues you with big enemies who take some whittling down before they die and will catch up unless you keep them at arm's length by using B to set a solid pace.

Boss design, finally, plays on each of these themes one by one. The first boss, for example, sits in the middle of the screen rotating his surroundings (including obstacles that you have to dodge), and you have to whack things with your boxing glove so they tumble into his command console and kill him off. In a sense, it's not just one good puzzle game idea, but a group of them built around a simple, almost faultlessly executed premise.

Increasingly fowl?
------------------

![Image 4](https://www.eurogamer.net/4_OmaElFs.jpg)

Or it would be, if it weren't for the fact that it isn't faultlessly executed at all. Heading into the main puzzle mode we easily steamrollered through much of the game in one evening, pausing to catch our breath and realising we were only a stone's throw from the final boss. The problems begin with the design of the levels. While they do challenge you from time to time, and gathering all the treasure will keep you busy, the vast majority yielded 100 per cent of their wares to us on the first go. Only a fraction of them needed us to run through them more than once or twice to obtain everything, and even the bosses rarely took more than a couple of tries. Even if your mileage does vary, surely it won't by the sort of margin required to stretch Kururin Squash out over more than a Sunday afternoon.

Ironically, as much as we owe this failing to lenient level design, superior controls are also to blame. The digital response of the GBA titles often made it harder, but the analogue control here is deadly smooth. The stick goes precisely where you want it to go and allows for much finer control through tricky situations, while the levels don't clamp down on you to compensate.

We also feel that it was slightly misguided to flesh it all out with the racing mode bit, even if it has worked before. It's more Time Trial in its approach than anything else, with levels unlocked more or less from the get-go, and arguably could have done with losing the checkpoints to up the ante and giving us multiple, staggered goal times to aspire to instead. We would have preferred twice as many regular puzzle levels to this against-the-clock stuff, really, and as a multiplayer mode it only works when all the players are at a similar skill level. Admittedly getting to a similar level isn't massively difficult, but how likely is it as a regular pick-up game with that in mind? And, while we're on the attack, we never did shake the feeling that, while attempts to break free of the central spinny evasion idea are admirable, they never really do as much for us as the pure alternative.

Finally the deathmatch mode. Initially we thought it was a bit unbalanced. It does, after all, combine a number of power-ups that were designed for the single-player game and then thrown together without warning. But in time it reveals itself to be a more Monkey Target-esque luck of the draw scenario, and with four players it can be manic. It's got a certain charm about it, that's for sure. But as for whether it's manic enough to displace the likes of Monkey Ball and Mario Kart in the grand scheme of Cube party pieces, we have our doubts. More likely it's half an hour's entertainment halfway through an evening in with your mates.

Contorted
---------

The net result of which is that you'll have tremendous fun playing Kururin Squash while it lasts, but that for all its improvements and clever ideas it's let down by an unfortunate shortfall in the quantity and quality of its levels. It just doesn't push you hard enough or for long enough, and the extras (also including a throwaway downloadable GBA mini-game) don't add much. In the end it's not worth what it'll probably cost you to import (despite its budget price point in Japan, you're bound to encounter import mark-up), and while we'd dearly love to see things like this cross the void between Japan and the West, it's hard to recommend this one particularly. If you've not played Kururin before, you should, but unless you haven't got a Game Boy you should look for Kuru Kuru Kururin or the Japanese sequel Kururin Paradise on eBay instead.

That said, if you are a Kururin vet and happen to stumble across Squash for £16 while trawling importers on a darkening afternoon in Soho as we did, it's an evening of all the beautiful, quirkily executed ideas from which are modern story-driven third-person action-blockbuster wotsits were originally derived, calling for speedy reactions and a touch of lateral thinking, and you will have fun. Just not enough of it. In other words, it'll captivate you for as long as it lasts, but don't be surprised if it then spins off onto a shelf with only a duck in a helicopter's chance of ever returning to the fore.

Kururin Squash!
===============

Posted by [Kurt Kalata](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/author/kurt/) on May 18, 2010

![Image 2](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-07.png)

#### Kururin Squash! (くるりんスカッシュ!) - GameCube (October 14, 2004)

  

This entry is part 3 of 3 in the series [Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/series/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")

  
[Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/series/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")

*   [Kuru Kuru Kururin](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/kuru-kuru-kururin/ "Kuru Kuru Kururin")
*   [Kururin Paradise](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/kururin-paradise/ "Kururin Paradise")
*   Kururin Squash!

[![Image 4](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-259x360.jpg)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash.jpg)

Kururin’s only console installment utilizes 3D graphics while keeping the same 2D mechanics. The visuals aren’t technically all that impressive (cel shaded polygons similar to the style of _Kururin Paradise_ would have been nicer), but they’re colorful and still plenty attractive. In the cutscenes, Kururin and pals are rendered as little cardboard puppets held on sticks, making for some pretty amusing cutscenes reminiscent of a kid’s TV show. Beyond the graphics, the real advantage of being on a TV screen is that the field of vision is much wider, and the view isn’t nearly as cramped as it was in the GBA games. Although it doesn’t utilize true analog control (you still need to press B to speed up), the GameCube controller is much smoother than the GBA directional pad.

[![Image 6](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-02-480x360.png)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-02.png)

While the alternate paths from _Kururin Paradise_ have been removed, each stage is now littered with coins. In order to get a perfect rating on a stage, you need to collect all coins in addition to reaching the exit without getting hit. Naturally, the stages can get pretty big, and you’ll need to cover every precarious nook and cranny to get 100%. You can also use these coins to buy a variety of items. Like the original, there are lots of useless things, like different Helirin skins or the ability to customize your life meter, but you can also buy maps, extra hearts, and an item that lets you continue from a checkpoint if you lose. There are also tons of super play videos to purchase.

In addition to the standard Helirin, there are now several different kinds of ships. One Helirin has boxing gloves at each end to knock around foes. Another has a pair of lasers. One can twirl around and shoot out miniature hurricanes, which can be used to push objects or block flame jets. Another lets you dive underwater, challenging you to dodge objects both above and below the surface. Most of these play similarly to the regular stages, but there’s also one where Helirin rides on a rail and can shoot flames out of its rotating blades. In addition to these new ships, there are still plenty of stages in the classic style. At the end of each world, you need to fight a boss battle using one of these new Helirins, challenging you at the skills you’ve learned throughout each zone. Including these boss levels, there are a total of forty stages in the Adventure mode of _Kururin Squash_. With the ability to use the items, most of these are quite easy, especially compared to _Kururin Paradise_. There are once again plenty of Challenge levels, but these are pretty short, as always. The multiplayer options are limited to a Race mode (similar to the first game) and a Battle mode, where up to four people beat each other up for coins. There’s also a Game Boy Advance mini game that can be played with the GBA link cable, but it’s a pretty crappy matching game.

[![Image 8](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-08-480x360.png)](http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/squash-08.png)

Once again, _Kururin Squash_ stayed in Japan, although it’s quite cheap and easy to obtain. Just beware that playing on a non-Japanese GameCube with a Freeloader will cause most of the text to become garbled. Navigating menus is easy, but all of the plot scenes and item descriptions will be unreadable.

11.title: S3VydXJpbiBTcXVhc2gh
11.content:
Exhilarating action while spinning!

*   JP release: 14th October 2004
*   EU release: N/A
*   NA release: N/A
*   Developer: Eighting
*   Publisher: Nintendo
*   NGC Magazine Score: 81%
*   Mods Used: Widescreen Code

![Image 1](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/kururinsquash-box-l.jpg)

![Image 2](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_22-45-01.jpg)

A sequel to the popular Game Boy Advance game Kuru Kuru Kururin. The series was made by Eighting, who made almost exclusively fighting games at the time, such as the Bloody Roar series. One of the many examples of a developer working with Nintendo to make something very different. After this GameCube Kuririn game, they wouldn’t work with Nintendo again until they ported Pikmin 3 to Switch and co-developed Pikmin 4.

![Image 3](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_21-41-51.jpg)

Like the other Kururin games, you control a spinning stick as you navigate mazes. It’s something that sounds simple but is immensely difficult, as the rotation of the stick will alter how difficult certain bends are. Levels have gimmicks to change things up, the simplest one being springs that let you change the direction of the spin.

![Image 4](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_21-54-50.jpg)

Some levels have unique features, too, such as water levels that let you dive to avoid obstacles, essentially giving you two layers of obstacles. There’s also some where you’re stuck to a rail while you control a flamethrower by spinning the stick – I didn’t like these at all, but the rest of the levels were great. There’s a surprising amount of variety for such a simple concept and it’s frustrating but fair.

![Image 5](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_21-27-23.jpg)

Some levels even add weapons to your stick, either large fists that punch out or, later on, guns to fire. You have to time attacking enemies with the spin of your stick, and I found the simple combat to be engaging due to the puzzle elements. At the end of each series of levels is a wonderful little boss fight. It’s all really cute and enjoyable.

![Image 6](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_21-41-19.jpg)

You can either play each level aiming for the best time or hunt for all the coins hidden in the level, which requires a bit of exploration and killing all enemies. These can be used to buy extra health, new UI designs or a GBA link cable game, which is a simple quiz where the GBA shows you a picture and you have to match it to one on the TV screen.

![Image 7](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GKQJ01_2025-11-08_21-18-59.jpg)

Considering the popularity of the GBA game and how there’s not much text you need to understand Kururin Squash, I’d imagine it was quite a popular import. I think it’s strange that Nintendo never released it outside of Japan.

![Image 8](https://djcube.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/greatn64.png)

**Great**

> Like Super Monkey Ball, there’s something superbly simple about Kururin Squash. Just as Sega’s masterpiece can be reduced to a high-concept pitch, so it is with Nintendo’s puzzling beauty.
> 
> Jes Bickham, NGC Magazine #101

**Remake or remaster?**

A remastered collection of the three Kururin games would be great.

**Official Ways to get the game**

There’s no official way to get Kururin Squash.

10.content:
[![Image 1: Kat Koller](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*ecTfLFSdLD0GToo32qqb2A.png)](https://medium.com/@katcolonel?source=post_page---byline--6953298ee61d---------------------------------------)

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 2](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*7E1C0-g2_-ICpIYS4_6YPg.png)

Balancing difficulty with fun can be a challenge in and of itself. An easy game can be enjoyed by players of any skill level, but it’s easy to look back on it and wish it could’ve been a bit more; a hard game can either feel extremely satisfying to beat, or put up a huge wall that some people will get exhausted of slamming their heads against. But what makes a game hard? Is it swarms of merciless enemies unceasingly firing on a single, helpless player? Is it high-intensity one-on-one combat? Is it platforming where if you simply take one hit, you die?

Well, if Kururin has anything to say about it, it’s mostly claustrophobia.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 3](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*a2ObXYkk4OzaRxYaqjdbZw.png)

Released in 2004 by Eighting, (formerly Eighting/Raizing, creators of Battle Garegga and Armed Police Batrider,) Kururin Squash is the third game in the Kururin trilogy. I’ll skip talking about the first two games because I can summarize my thoughts as, they’re good, but they don’t have much on Squash.

The core design of Kururin is simple: You control a flying machine with revolving wings, and you have to fly through mazes without slamming into walls or obstacles. Frequently, you’ll find blue springs that reverse your rotation so you can squeeze through different gaps. Kururin Squash doesn’t deviate from this core design, and by far I’d say it’s the best execution of it I’ve seen, well, ever.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 4](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*P_SQrOxl9CIG5wJ4TTJUBg.png)

Kururin Squash’s success lies in its level design, which is easily the strongest of the series barring maybe some of the stages in Paradise. Most of the levels are the same basic gameplay as always, but with more screen space and tighter movement, managing yourself is a lot easier. You can see further ahead, and just have an easier time stopping before you smack your head against something. Even towards the end of the game, when it starts throwing some seriously tight curved pathways at you that you have to snake through, it never feels impossible, just really tense.

What’s maybe more notable about Squash, though, is its fresh inclusion of gimmick levels that totally shake up the basic design of the game, without losing the core focus.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 5](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*Zc_lWOA_d8aJ2PEZsn_BEA.png)

Largely, these levels are actually extremely successful at what they set out to do, partially thanks to just the sheer variety of gimmicks on display. Every world has its own gimmick, every gimmick emphasizes something different, and no world has more than three of these levels. The result is something genuinely good at breaking the pace of the regular game that never overstays its welcome.

The gimmicks at play at their simplest revolve around punching enemies with boxing gloves and blasting them down with lasers, but the most interesting to me are world 2’s submarine stages that task you with raising and lowering between two layers to avoid hitting obstacles and to turn switches, world 3’s flamethrower stages that put you on rails and make you rotate to aim at enemies along the track while also spinning to avoid slamming into large crystals, and world 4’s propeller stages where your wings can be sped up fast enough to create gusts of air that can protect you from flames and launch away enemies.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 6](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*cw5eeJW7Lo8zVFmjSJ_VIA.png)

All three of these gimmicks either build on the foundation of Kururin, or add a twist so unique and satisfying that it almost feels like a different game. I wouldn’t want Squash to focus purely on any of them, but I’m glad it explored them. If I had to give one complaint though, it’s that the submarine stages are the only gimmick the game comes up with that don’t emphasize combat in some way, which is odd for Kururin, being a very relaxed series that at the start didn’t even really have a villain to speak of.

Get Kat Koller’s stories in your inbox
--------------------------------------

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

One aspect shared by both the normal stages and the gimmick stages, though, is coins, which also happen to be one of Squash’s newest and perhaps most important additions.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 7](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*YXlJpfAMPdJiQrjKPnc21A.png)

Coins can be collected to be used at shops in each world, mostly to buy new skins and HUDs, or for temporary HP boosters or strategy videos for individual stages. While the ability to buy HP boosts is definitely a decent way to give less skilled players some leeway, one could argue that skins being bumped from hidden collectibles to shop items is a bit of a disappointment, and I could definitely understand that.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 8](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*FbN4jLHmIDGsaN9ieIEnGw.png)

But if I’m being honest, I think coins are a very important addition to Squash’s level design. Not only do they allow it to justify having more small hidden pockets to snake around lending stages more play time, but more importantly, it allows the game to more consistently incentivize taking risks, give the player more of a clear path to follow, and generally just feels pretty satisfying on its own.

Speaking of snaking around, I have to give special praise to the controls in Kururin Squash. It’s the first Kururin game to be released on a system with an actual analog stick, and I don’t think it would even be half as good otherwise. For everything Kuru Kuru Kururin and Kururin Paradise do well, I can’t play them without feeling ridiculously clumsy or frustrated, and I think that’s because a D-pad just isn’t a very good fit for the game’s design.

In contrast, the analog movement in Kururin Squash is so precise, there are times where it feels like the level design couldn’t be half as good as it is without the controls to back it up. You still need to hold B to move a bit faster, but in effect that gives you an extra handy way to manage your own speed, which is a good fit for Squash’s level design.

And maybe most importantly, Squash carries over Paradise’s addition of having the right shoulder button speed up your rotation. With the GameCube’s analog triggers, though, this goes from letting you switch between two speeds to making finer adjustments to your turn speed by however much you need at a given moment. Combined with the tighter movement, Squash really does feel the most freeing of the trilogy in terms of how it plays. Just moving around in this game is really a joy.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 9](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*6S88hPd0hsIC1Ry63FnQ2w.png)

There is one last addition in Squash, and it’s the boss stages. They’re alright? They generally build around the world gimmicks in ways that are decently fun, but only a couple of them really feel like a strong enough divergence from the regular stages. The final boss in particular is a bit disappointing, but a part of that is admittedly just because the final world’s gimmick is comparatively underwhelming as a whole.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 10](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*P8aTPvhIpkXkC0vsXY9KuQ.png)

When it comes to presentation, though, Kururin Squash is very charming. It’s clearly not a big budget game, and absolutely not big enough to have much in the way of animated cutscenes, but the way the developers go about this while maintaining the colorful presentation of Kururin is pretty fantastic, opting for a comical paper cut-out puppet theater aesthetic. It’s cute, it works! Holds up better than some other 2004 titles.

The soundtrack of Kururin Squash is also pretty solid, composed by series composer Atsuhiro Motoyama, who may be better known for his work on Umihara Kawase and Battle Bakraid. Most of the music is in a similar low-key, relaxed pop style as the other games, but at the very end it dips into an intense rock style, and the boss theme is a very heavy and bass-y electronic track, both of which call back more to Raizing’s old shooters more than anything, funny enough.

All in all, Kururin Squash is a game I would easily recommend playing. It’s extremely unique gameplay is something I’ve only really seen an attempt to replicate more recently in 2016's Roundabout, and for all of Roundabout’s strengths, I still think Kururin Squash is handily the best game at what it does, just in terms of pure design and mechanics.

Kururin Squash was the last Kururin game to ever be released, but Eighting’s still managed to have a bit of a history since then. Fans of fighting games, Fate, or both might know them as the developers of the 2008 fighting game Fate/unlimited codes, otherwise known as “Fuc”. Their library of fighting games actually extends even further than that, though, as the co-developers of Castlevania Judgment, and developers of Tatsunoko vs Capcom, and Marvel vs Capcom 3. If you’re familiar with trashy licensed anime fighting games, you might even know them for a few, including the classic game that took Super Smash Bros Melee by surprise, Battle Stadium DON.

These days, though, Eighting seems to take more of an assisting role, with their most notable work being assisting Capcom in developing Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate and 4 Ultimate. No need to worry about them, though. They’re just making Kamen Rider games now.

Once again, thanks to everyone pledging and supporting me in making these posts on [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/colonelreviewsgamesorsomething)! I don’t have any plans to lock any of these posts behind supporting me, so it’s really your own choice whether or not you want to. If you do, I appreciate it, but either way, thank you for reading!

8.   [Board](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/boards/922054-kururin-squash)

Kururin Squash is one of those odd games that really can’t be fully understood until one plays the game for himself. Navigating a rotating stick through a labyrinth… That’s the basic concept of this game. It may sound simplistic at first, but in actuality, the Kururin series is all about making even the most frustratingly tangled levels a whole lot of fun.
**Gameplay: 9/10**

This is what makes the Kururin series so unique. There isn’t another game quite like it on the entire videogame market! In Kururin Squash, you control a rotating stick that you must navigate through a sprawling maze. Sound simple? It’s not! Each time you travel through a bend in the maze, you have to coordinate the rotation of the ship with the layout of the level so you don’t hit any walls on the way through. Sure, that alone becomes pretty easy after a few levels… But that’s where morning star cannonballs, blazing flames, and rabid fish come in! Each of these adds moving elements to the levels, forcing you to make more rapid ‘on the fly’ decisions.

To add a bit of deviation to the gameplay, every couple of levels, you will be treated to a special variation of your standard rotating stick. In some levels, you’ll have punching gloves on your vehicle to attack enemies; in others, you’ll get to pilot a submarine, meaning you will have to worry about two levels at once: above water and underwater! In addition to the standard levels, there are bosses every so often that will test your ability to use the special powered-up ships.

**Controls: 10/10**

Put simply, the controls for this game make sense. The analog stick moves your ship through the levels. The R button speeds up its rotation, while the B button pushes your ship through the level a little faster. In instances where you have a special ability attached to your ship, the A button activates it. The controls really couldn’t be any easier to understand.

**Graphics: 10/10**

This game is absolutely beautiful. I couldn’t ask for better graphics in this type of a game. The mazes themselves look wonderful, with no jagged or blocky walls appearing anywhere. The backgrounds that lie behind the mazes are pleasant as well, all being detailed and highly animated.

**Sound/Music: 8/10**

Nothing to complain about here! There aren’t many sound effects in this game (hardly any places to put them, other than hitting walls, for example), but the ones that _are_ there fit the game perfectly. The music is marvelously constructed and quite soothing. You won’t be humming the tunes for hours on end after you power off your system, but you won’t want to mute the television during gameplay, either.

**Multiplayer: 7/10**

This game offers enough fun with its single-player mode alone, but if you have friends who’d like to play with you for a bit, there’s fun to be had here. There is a plethora of specially designed levels for racing through with friends (sorry Kururin vets… you can’t play through the single-player maps here, but I think these special levels more than make up for it). There is also a fighting minigame (with several of its own levels) where you’re pitted against your friends on a rectangular playing field and must attack them with various power-ups to steal their coins (if you’ve played Super Monkey Ball, think Monkey Fight!). And for those of us with enough GameBoy Advances and GBA-GCN link cables: A mode where you can play GBA-GCN minigames with your friends. Not the deepest gameplay, but it’s a little fun in ten minute segments.

**Replay Value: 8/10**

Kururin Squash has a fair amount of replay value. It’s a short game if you just blast through all the levels and leave it at that, but this game is about getting higher scores. Collecting all the coins in each level, completing the levels without hitting any walls at all, and beating the top speeds will all take a decent amount of time and will earn you in-game rewards. There are extra ships and screen layouts that can be purchased in the game with the coins you collect in each level. Collecting enough coins to purchase everything can take awhile, as well. Of course, if you have friends to play this game with, that will also extend the game’s replay value.

**”I have the other Kururin games. How does this compare?”**

If you’ve played the GBA Kururin games to death (especially Kururin Paradise), Squash will probably seem a little easy. Also, compared to the expansive multiplayer modes in Paradise, this game is severely lacking in the multiplayer department. However, with all of the fun elements new to this game (mainly, ship power-ups and bosses), I’d say Squash is still worth looking into.

**Import Friendly?**

_Very_ import friendly. The order of the menu options makes complete sense. It won’t take more than two minutes to get into the game for the first time. If you’ve never played a Kururin game before, it’s more than worth importing to try out the totally unique gameplay.

**Final Score (not an average): 8/10**

3.content:
_**This page contains story spoilers.**_

_Kururin Squash!_ is the third and final game in the Kururin series. It was released for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube) on October 14th, 2004. Unlike its predecessors, _Kururin Squash!_ has never been rereleased, and remains exclusive to the GameCube.

[![Image 1](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/f/f4/Kururin_Squash%21_Coverart.jpg)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Kururin_Squash!_Coverart.jpg)

Coverart of Kururin Squash!

The story follows [Kururin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Kururin "Kururin"), who was on a free family vacation his family won. However, when Kururin gets home, he notices all his siblings are gone. Professor Isogashima had captured them, and he built several robots to stop Kururin from "interfering with his research". After Kururin rescues all his siblings, he goes home, but his father, Totorin, is not there. Isogashima had kidnapped him in Wonderverse, the final level in the game. So Kururin rides the [Helirin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helirin "Helirin") to save him. Beatable "Dad" times on each level are unlocked after rescuing Totorin. Throughout the game, Teacher Hare invents new Helirins to help Kururin progress.

[![Image 2](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/thumb/c/c1/Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png/300px-Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Why_are_you_catching_my_brothers%3F.png)

A screenshot of the first cutscene of the NewGBAXL English translation patch of Kururin Squash!

The gameplay is similar to the prior 2 games. You control the [Helirin](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helirin "Helirin"), an automatically spinning stick, through tight mazes. When Helirin hits the wall, you lose a heart. When you lose all 3 (5 if a Heart-Up is used) hearts, Helirin shatters and the level must be restarted, or, if an Amazing Heart is used, restart from the last heart panel. By pressing the B button, Helirin will move faster and by pressing the R button, Helirin will rotate faster. There are blue springs throughout the levels that will cause Helirin to rotate in the opposite direction it's currently rotating in. New to this game, are five Helirins, [Helibokaan](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibokaan "Helibokaan"), [Helibashan](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibashan "Helibashan"), [Heliboboh](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Heliboboh "Heliboboh"), [Heliburuun](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Heliburuun "Heliburuun"), and [Helibibyuun](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/Helibibyuun "Helibibyuun"). The Helibokaan (Helibash in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Sweet Shores. When the A button is pressed, the boxing gloves on both end of it will extend, and it will punch through obstacles and enemies, rewarding the player with coins. The Helibashan (Helibubble in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Coastal Canopy. When the A button is pressed, Helibashan will go underwater until either the A button is released, or when air runs out. The Heliboboh (Heliblaze in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Snowscape. When the A button is pressed, flames will released from either side, which will kill enemies. If you dash with the B button, the flames get longer. The Heliburuun (Heliblow in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in CyberCity. If you hold the A button long enough, when you let go, a tornado will be released that can kill enemies, reveal areas obscured by smoke, and block fire. The Helibibyuun (Helibeam in the NewGBAXL patch) is used in some levels in Wonderverse. When the A button is pressed, lasers will shoot out of either side of it. These lasers kill enemies and can shoot bombs. At the end of each world, you fight a boss with the Helirin used in that level.

[![Image 3](https://static.wikitide.net/kururinwiki/thumb/2/22/Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png/300px-Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png)](https://kururin.miraheze.org/wiki/File:Sweet_Shores_4_Screenshot.png)

A screenshot of the level Sweet Shores 4.
